tips.title: Use the specification's two phrases
tips.body: System software **manages the computer system resources** and **acts as a platform to run application software**. Application software **performs end-user tasks**. A paraphrase often drops the *platform* half, which is the half that explains why applications need it.

tips.title: A job for the user, or for the computer?
tips.body: One question classifies anything. A word processor writes your letter: **application**. A defragmenter tidies the disk: **system**. Ask it consistently and borderline cases stop being guesswork.

tips.title: Count to five for the OS
tips.body: Processor, memory, I/O devices, applications, **security**. Security is the one people leave off, and it is a separate mark. If the question says *functions*, plural, make sure you have all five.

tips.title: Judge by purpose, not by origin
tips.body: A **web browser** ships with the operating system but is still **application** software, because browsing is an end-user task. Where software came from tells you nothing about what it is for.

tips.title: Utilities are maintenance
tips.body: Defragmentation, backup, compression, anti-malware and encryption are one idea, not five facts: they **maintain the system** rather than doing a task for the user. That is why they are all system software.

steps.title: Hardware and software
steps.body:
Two definitions, and the relationship between them.

**Hardware** is the **physical** parts of a computer system — the parts you could pick up. The processor, the memory, the hard disk, the keyboard, the screen, the cables.

**Software** is the **programs and data** that run on the hardware. It has no physical existence of its own: it is instructions, stored as patterns in memory or on a disk.

**The relationship** is what the specification actually asks for, so it is worth stating properly:

$$\textbf{Hardware cannot do anything useful without software to tell it what to do, and software cannot run without hardware to run on.}$$

Each is useless alone. A processor with no program sits idle; a program with no processor is just a pattern of bits on a disk.

A test that settles most examples: **could you drop it on your foot?** If yes, it is hardware. A DVD is hardware; the film stored on it is not. A USB stick is hardware; the files on it are software or data.

steps.title: System software and application software
steps.body:
All software divides into two kinds, and the distinction is about **who it is for**.

**System software** **manages the computer system's resources** and **acts as a platform to run application software**. It works for the **computer**.

Examples: the **operating system**, **utility programs**, **device drivers**.

**Application software** is software that **performs end-user tasks**. It works for the **person**.

Examples: a **word processor**, a **web browser**, a **spreadsheet**, a **game**, a **photo editor**.

Those two phrases — *manages the computer system resources and acts as a platform*, and *performs end-user tasks* — come straight from the specification and are what the marks are for.

**How to classify anything.** Ask: **does this do a job for the user, or a job for the computer?** A word processor writes a letter for you: **application**. A disk defragmenter tidies the hard disk so everything runs better: **system**. 

The one people hesitate over is a **web browser**. It feels like part of the computer because it is always there — but it performs an **end-user task**, browsing the web, so it is **application** software.

steps.title: The operating system
steps.body:
The **operating system** is the most important piece of system software. Without it a computer would start up and do nothing, because nothing else would have a platform to run on.

The specification lists **five** things the OS manages, and a question asking for its functions expects them:

- the **processor(s)** — deciding which program runs next and for how long, so several can appear to run at once
- **memory** — deciding where each program's data goes and stopping one program overwriting another's
- **input/output (I/O) devices** — handling the keyboard, screen, printer and disks so applications do not each need their own code for every device
- **applications** — starting them, stopping them, and providing the services they call on
- **security** — user accounts, passwords and permissions, controlling who may do what

A good way to hold them: **processor, memory, devices, applications, security**. Five, and the last is the one most often forgotten.

**Utility programs** are the other kind of system software. They perform **maintenance tasks** that keep the system working well rather than doing anything for the user directly:

- **defragmentation** — reorganising files on a disk so they are stored contiguously and read faster
- **compression** — making files smaller so they take less space
- **backup** — copying data so it can be recovered if lost
- **anti-malware** — detecting and removing malicious software
- **encryption** — scrambling data so it cannot be read without the key

steps.title: Why the operating system matters
steps.body:
It is worth understanding **why** an operating system exists, because it turns a list of five functions into one idea.

Without an OS, **every application would have to do all of it itself**. A word processor would need its own code for every model of printer, its own way of finding space in memory, its own scheme for sharing the processor with whatever else was running. Every application would need that code, and they would conflict with each other constantly.

The OS solves this by doing those jobs **once, centrally**, and offering them as services. That is what the specification means by:

$$\textbf{system software ... acts as a platform to run application software}$$

A **platform**: something applications are built on top of, and can rely on.

Two consequences follow, and both are examinable:

- **Applications become much simpler.** They ask the OS to print, and the OS deals with the printer. The application does not need to know what kind of printer it is.
- **Programs are kept apart.** Because the OS manages memory, one program cannot overwrite another's data, so a crash in one need not take the whole machine down.

That second point is also why **security** belongs in the OS's list. It is the only software positioned to control what every other program may do.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Define hardware and software.
2. Explain the relationship between them.
3. Give two examples of system software and two of application software.

**Part B.**

4. What does the specification say system software does? Use its own two phrases.
5. List the five things an operating system manages.
6. Name three utility programs and say what each does.

**Part C.**

7. Classify each of these and give a reason: a web browser, a disk defragmenter, a compiler, a game.
8. Explain why an operating system makes applications simpler to write.

For question 7, ask the same question each time: does it do a job for the **user** or for the **computer**?

steps.title: Going deeper: the phrases the marks are for
steps.body:
**Use the specification's own wording.** Two phrases are worth learning verbatim, because a paraphrase often loses the mark:

- System software **manages the computer system resources** and **acts as a platform to run application software**.
- Application software **performs end-user tasks**.

*System software is the stuff that runs the computer* gets across the idea but misses both halves — particularly the **platform** half, which is what explains why applications need it.

**The five OS functions.** Processor, memory, I/O devices, applications, **security**. Security is the one most often left off, and it is a separate mark. If a question asks for *the functions of an operating system*, count to five.

**Where classification gets hard.** Three cases catch people:

- A **web browser** feels like part of the system because it comes installed. But it performs an **end-user task**, so it is an **application**. Ask what it is *for*, not where it came from.
- A **compiler** translates code. That is a job for a **programmer** — an end user of that tool — so it is usually classed as **application** software, though it is close to the system. If a question asks, explain your reasoning; that is what is being marked.
- **Anti-virus** does something the user wants, but its job is **maintaining the system**, so it is a **utility** and therefore **system** software.

The lesson is that the boundary is about **purpose**, and a borderline case is best answered with the reason as well as the label.

**Hardware and software need each other.** The relationship is a **two-way** dependency and the mark scheme usually wants both directions: hardware without software does nothing useful, and software without hardware cannot run at all. Giving only one direction gives half the answer.

**Utilities are maintenance.** They keep the system working well rather than producing anything for the user. That single idea — **maintenance, not user tasks** — tells you that defragmentation, backup, compression, encryption and anti-malware all belong together, rather than being five separate facts.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Hardware** is the **physical** parts of a computer system; **software** is the **programs and data** that run on it.
- The relationship runs **both ways**: hardware does nothing useful without software, and software cannot run without hardware.
- **System software** **manages the computer system resources** and **acts as a platform to run application software**.
- **Application software** **performs end-user tasks**.
- To classify anything, ask: **a job for the user, or for the computer?**
- A **web browser** is an **application**, however built-in it feels — it performs an end-user task.
- The **operating system** manages the **processor(s)**, **memory**, **I/O devices**, **applications** and **security**.
- **Security is the fifth**, and the one most often forgotten.
- **Utility programs** do **maintenance**: defragmentation, compression, backup, anti-malware, encryption.
- Without an OS, every application would need its own code for every device and would conflict with the others.
- The OS does those jobs **once, centrally**, which is what **platform** means.
- For a borderline case, give the **reason** as well as the label.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between system software and application software, giving two examples of each, and explain how you would classify a piece of software you had not met before.
questions.solution: System software is software that manages the resources of the computer system and acts as a platform on which application software can run. Two examples of system software are the operating system, which manages the processor, memory, input and output devices, applications and security, and utility programs such as a disk defragmenter or an anti-virus program, which carry out maintenance tasks that keep the system working well. Application software, by contrast, is software that performs end-user tasks, meaning tasks that the person using the computer wants done. Two examples are a word processor, which is used to write documents, and a web browser, which is used to view web pages. To classify a piece of software that I had not met before, I would ask a single question about its purpose: does it do a job for the user, or does it do a job for the computer? If it produces something the user wants, such as a document or an edited photograph, it is application software. If it manages the system's resources or maintains the system so that other software can run properly, it is system software. It is important to judge by purpose rather than by where the software came from, because a web browser that is installed with the operating system is still application software, since browsing the web is an end-user task.

questions.modelAnswer:
**System software** **manages the computer system resources** and **acts as a platform to run application software**.

*Examples:* the **operating system**, which manages the processor, memory, I/O devices, applications and security; and **utility programs** such as a disk defragmenter or anti-virus, which carry out **maintenance**.

**Application software** **performs end-user tasks** — jobs the person wants done.

*Examples:* a **word processor**, for writing documents; a **web browser**, for viewing web pages.

**Classifying something new.** Ask one question about its **purpose**:

> Does it do a job for the **user**, or a job for the **computer**?

If it produces something the user wants — a document, an edited photo — it is **application**. If it manages resources or maintains the system so other software runs properly, it is **system**.

**Judge by purpose, not origin.** A web browser installed with the operating system is still **application** software, because browsing the web is an end-user task. Where software came from tells you nothing about what it is for.

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of an operating system, and explain why applications would be much harder to write without one.
questions.solution: An operating system manages five things. It manages the processor or processors, deciding which program should run next and for how long, so that several programs can appear to run at the same time. It manages memory, deciding where each program's data is placed and keeping programs separate so that one cannot overwrite another's data. It manages input and output devices, handling the keyboard, the screen, the printer and the disks. It manages applications, starting them, stopping them and providing services that they can call upon. Finally it manages security, through user accounts, passwords and permissions, controlling what each user and each program is allowed to do. Without an operating system, every application would have to carry out all of these jobs for itself. A word processor would need its own code for every model of printer it might ever be connected to, it would have to find its own space in memory, and it would have to compete directly with every other running program for the processor. Every application would duplicate the same work, and because each would be doing it independently they would frequently conflict with one another. The operating system solves this by performing these jobs once, centrally, and offering them to applications as services, which is exactly what is meant by saying that system software acts as a platform on which application software runs.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The five functions.**

- **The processor(s)** — deciding which program runs next and for how long, so several appear to run at once.
- **Memory** — placing each program's data and **keeping programs apart**, so one cannot overwrite another's.
- **Input/output devices** — handling the keyboard, screen, printer and disks.
- **Applications** — starting and stopping them, and providing services they call on.
- **Security** — user accounts, passwords and permissions, controlling what each user and program may do.

Security is the one most often left off, and it is a separate mark.

**Without an operating system.** Every application would have to do **all of that itself**:

- a word processor would need its own code for **every model of printer**
- it would have to find its own space in **memory**
- it would have to compete directly for the **processor**

Every application would duplicate the same work, and doing it independently they would **conflict** constantly.

**What the OS does instead.** It performs those jobs **once, centrally**, and offers them as **services**. That is exactly what the specification means by *system software acts as a platform to run application software*.

examTechnique.body:
Use the specification's wording for the two kinds of software, including the platform half for system software.

When defining hardware and software, give the relationship in both directions.

For the functions of an operating system, give all five and make sure security is one of them.

When classifying, state the label and the reason. For a borderline case the reasoning is what is being marked.

Judge software by what it is for, not by whether it came installed.

Group the utilities as maintenance rather than listing them as unrelated facts.
examinerErrors: Defining system software without mentioning that it acts as a platform.
Giving only one direction of the hardware and software relationship.
Leaving security out of the operating system's functions.
Classifying a web browser as system software because it comes installed.
Calling a device driver application software.
Saying an operating system makes the computer faster, rather than managing resources.
Giving a classification with no reason where a reason was asked for.
Describing a utility as something the user runs to get a job done.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer uses the specification's own phrases and includes the platform half, which is what makes the rest of the topic make sense. It gives all five operating system functions without prompting, security included. Classifying software, it applies one consistent test about purpose and gives the reason alongside the label, so a borderline case like a compiler is answered rather than guessed. And it can explain why an operating system exists at all — that without one every application would duplicate the same work and conflict with the others — rather than listing functions as unconnected facts.
